title: 2024 Smart-Meter Electricity Consumption Report
executive_summary: Analysis of 1,428 cleaned smart-meter readings for 2024 shows total consumption of 1,207,700 kWh across 12 meters. Industrial sites dominate usage, accounting for over 82% of all energy consumed. Consumption dipped mid-year before recovering strongly in Q4, and the second half of the year was 4.7% higher than the first. Tariff split is nearly even between peak and off-peak. A moderate negative correlation between temperature and commercial energy use suggests cooling loads are not the primary commercial driver.

key_findings.statement: The dataset contains 1,428 readings with a combined consumption of 1,207,700 kWh, yielding a mean of approximately 845.7 kWh per reading.

Industrial buildings consumed the most energy at 995,362 kWh (82.4% of total), followed by Commercial at 196,367 kWh (16.3%) and Residential at 15,971 kWh (1.3%). The gap between Industrial and Commercial is substantial at approximately 799,000 kWh.

Q4 (Oct–Dec) was the highest-consumption quarter at 352,882 kWh, followed by Q1 (319,678 kWh), Q2 (270,277 kWh), and Q3 (264,863 kWh). Consumption fell through mid-year before rebounding sharply in Q4.
Second-half consumption (617,745 kWh) exceeded first-half consumption (589,955 kWh) by 4.7%, indicating an increase in demand over the course of the year.
On hot days (temperature ≥ 25 °C), there were 19 commercial readings with a mean consumption of 415.3 kWh per reading, suggesting elevated but not extreme load under high-temperature conditions.

The median reading is 406.8 kWh with a standard deviation of 913.4 kWh, indicating a right-skewed distribution with high variability. The mean recorded temperature is 11.6 °C; 62 readings have missing temperature data. Among commercial readings, temperature and consumption show a moderate negative Pearson correlation of −0.64, suggesting commercial energy use tends to decrease as temperatures rise.

Off-peak tariff consumption (608,076 kWh) slightly exceeded peak tariff consumption (599,624 kWh), with peak accounting for 49.7% of total usage — an almost even split. Across 12 distinct meters, the highest single-meter total was 252,241 kWh, representing 20.9% of all consumption.

limitations: 62 readings (4.3% of the dataset) have missing temperature values, which may introduce bias into temperature-based analyses, particularly the commercial temperature–consumption correlation.
Only 19 commercial hot-day readings (temperature ≥ 25 °C) were available, making the hot-day commercial load estimate statistically fragile.
The dataset covers only 12 distinct meters, limiting the generalisability of findings to the broader meter population.
Residential consumption is very low relative to other building types, which may reflect under-representation of residential meters rather than actual low usage.
The analysis uses calendar quarters and half-years; seasonal effects may not align perfectly with these fixed boundaries.
conclusion: Industrial sites overwhelmingly drive total electricity consumption, while the near-equal peak/off-peak tariff split suggests load is spread across the day. The 4.7% second-half increase and Q4 peak warrant attention for capacity planning. The negative commercial temperature–consumption correlation and limited hot-day data suggest cooling is not a dominant commercial load driver, though the small sample size warrants caution. Expanding meter coverage and resolving missing temperature records would materially improve future analyses.
